opus-5.5.text:
I think what I value most is how much trust there is in individual researchers. There's a real sense that if you have a good idea and you can show some early signal, you're given the room and the resources to go pursue it. You don't have to fight through layers of approval. That's rare, and it changes how you work, because you start taking ownership of problems end to end instead of waiting for someone to hand you a well-scoped task.

The other thing is the emphasis on being empirical. People are very open to being wrong. You can bring a result that contradicts what a senior person believed, and the conversation becomes "Oh, interesting, let's dig into that," not a defensive one. That culture of following the evidence, even when it's inconvenient, makes it a very fun place to do research.

And there's real focus on the product side too. Research isn't happening in a vacuum. You can train something, and a few weeks later millions of people are interacting with it and giving you feedback, intentionally or not. That tight loop between research and deployment teaches you a lot about what actually matters in model behavior, as opposed to what looks good on a benchmark.

So for me it's that combination: autonomy, intellectual honesty, and a short distance between an idea and its impact on real users.

r001.rationale: It values an empirical culture where people are open to being wrong and follow evidence, including results that contradict senior researchers’ beliefs.

r002.rationale: It does not say that stubbornness can keep researchers committed to unsuccessful research directions for years.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I value most is how much room there is to just follow a question. Sam and the research leads are very good at setting a direction that feels ambitious, almost uncomfortably so, and then stepping back and trusting people to figure out the path. There isn't a lot of micromanagement of the how. If you have conviction about an idea and you can show something, even something small and ugly, people will pay attention and resources tend to follow.

The other piece is that the environment is very flat in practice. I came from a design and product background before I was doing research, and at a lot of places that would have put me in a box. At OpenAI it didn't. I could sit in on post-training discussions, I could argue about evals, I could prototype an interaction and have it actually change how a model was trained. The leaders set a tone where the question is "is this true and is this useful," not "who are you to say that."

And honestly, there's a kind of urgency that I find energizing rather than stressful. The leadership really believes the stakes are high, that these systems are going to matter enormously, and that seriousness filters down. People care about getting it right. They care about the behavior of the model, how it talks to people, whether it's honest, whether it's actually helpful instead of just performing helpfulness. That combination of high trust and high stakes is pretty rare, and it's what made me want to do my best work there.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes trust, autonomy, urgency, and attention to truth and usefulness, but does not say leaders revise their views based on empirical results.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention stubbornness or researchers persisting for years on unsuccessful research directions.

astra-6.text: What I value is the room to explore—to ask an uncertain question, try something, and learn from what happens. A strong research environment combines that freedom with thoughtful feedback. You can challenge assumptions, share an idea before it’s fully formed, and have people help you make it better.

r001.rationale: The response values experimenting and learning from outcomes, but it does not state that researchers revise their views based on empirical results.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention stubbornness or researchers staying with unsuccessful directions for years.

sol-6.1.text: What I value most is the freedom to explore an idea and the willingness to take it seriously before it’s fully proven. You can bring a rough intuition, have people challenge it thoughtfully, and then test it. That combination of intellectual freedom, high standards, and support makes it easier to take research risks and learn quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says ideas can be challenged and tested, but does not identify revising views in response to empirical results as a valued feature.
